subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF TASK FORCE REPORT ON UNIFICATION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43.
In the report of the Fyffe Task Force on Unification tabled by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne) on Friday, there were clearly identified nine major problem areas in the Department of National Defence and the armed forces. Furthermore, the task force made 30 concrete recommendations for the minister to implement in order to rectify these problems.
Bearing in mind the sanctimonious statement of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) last Friday when he claimed that the other parties did "not have the same respect for the role of the members of Parliament as we on this side", I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie):
That the Minister of National Defence make an order of reference to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence to examine the task force report on unification and to allow the minister, his senior officials and other interested parties to appear before that committee to explain how best to implement the 30 recommendations contained in the report, so that the serious problems in the armed forces can be rectified.

subsubtopic: RECOGNITION OF NATIONAL FOREST WEEK-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In recognition of the fact that over one million Canadian workers are either directly or indirectly employed by forest-related industries, that forest products' shipments exceed $21 billion annually, $12 billion of which is earned through the exports of finished and refined products, and that our forests provide a basis for a multi-billion dollar outdoor industry, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain):
That this House recognize the importance of our forests to our country's social and economic well-being, that it pay tribute to the workers and professionals who manage our forest heritage in the week of May 4 to May 10 which- sponsored by the Canadian Forestry Association-has been designated as National Forest Week, and that the government in the course of this week address particular attention to the difficulties which are presently experienced by our forest industries.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR IMMEDIATE STEPS TO ALLEVIATE URBAN RENTAL CRISIS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43.
In view of the fact that Canada is suffering from an acute shortage of rental accommodation which seriously affects many families and single parents in urban centres, and since the minister responsible for the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation has stated that this problem of rental housing ranks second in priority with his ministry, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell):
That the House instruct the minister to consider the shortage of rental accommodation as top priority and undertake immediate steps to alleviate the urban rental housing crisis.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I, too, rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Whereas the supplies of non-renewable fossil fuels, primarily oil and natural gas, are being depleted, but that there are still many forms of renewable energy provided by the sun, pollution-free and inexhaustible, and whereas the national chairman of the Solar Energy Society of Canada said in celebrating "Sun" day on Saturday, May 3, "The government makes all kinds of noises about conservation but doesn't do anything about it", I move, seconded by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton):
That this government should produce less talk on conservation and more action, and that as a first step allow federal tax rebates and incentives for solar hot water systems like the successful California programs of this type in the United States.

subsubtopic: LOCATION OF DVA OFFICES AT CHARLOTTETOWN, P.E.I.- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the fact the Government of Canada has announced that it intends to move the site for the relocated Department of Veterans Affairs from the Charlottetown waterfront to uptown, the centre of that city, and in view of the fact that the change in site will involve a very substantial breach by the federal government of a binding agreement between the federal government, the government of P.E.I. and the government of Charlottetown, through the Charlottetown Area Development Corporation, and in view of the fact that the uptown site is vigorously opposed both by the government of P.E.I. and the city council, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass):
That this House condemn the federal government for changing the site for the Department of Veterans Affairs in Charlottetown without consulting either the province of P.E.I. or the city of Charlottetown; and
That the House petition the government to proceed immediately with the relocation of the Department of Veterans Affairs on the basis of the waterfront site, the one the province of P.E.I. and the city favour.

speechtext:

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that the salmon fishery on Canada's west coast is one of our most valuable national resources, and since the Fraser and Thompson Rivers form the last of the major, unobstructed salmon migration and spawning systems in North America, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell):
That this House direct the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and the Minister of the Environment to use their considerable powers to provide assistance to communities in the Thompson drainage basin interested in establishing land disposal sewage treatment systems which would eliminate the present threat to this most valuable fishery.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT FINANCIAL SUPPORT FOR DREE PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance who, as we all know, is the Deputy Prime Minister. On Friday, his colleague the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion called regional disparities in Canada "a national disgrace". He went on to state that the financial resources of his department are stretched to the limit, and said there was "barely enough to honour the commitments made even by the previous Liberal government".
Given this extraordinary statement by his colleague, I wish to ask the minister why the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion is forced to make public the lack of government financial support for DREE, and why his government is now providing inadequate funds to fight for regional development in this country.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT FINANCIAL SUPPORT FOR DREE PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion is obviously taking his work very seriously, and is obviously carrying his pleas beyond the rooms of the cabinet. To that 1 have no objection.
I would point out that there is a very substantial amount of funds already available within that department. I happen to be a representative of a client in that area of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. There is no one more sympathetic to his requirements than I am. At the same time, the hon. member must realize that we are operating under a policy of fiscal restraint at the present time, and it is not possible to escalate projected expenditures in the way that each of us might like individually but which in total would have a very damaging effect on the size of the deficit, inflation and the Canadian economy as a whole.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT FINANCIAL SUPPORT FOR DREE PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, contrary to what the Minister of Finance says, the minister responsible says that there are inadequate funds, and points out that whereas in 1970 some 2 per cent of the federal budget was allocated to DREE, with the present government that has dropped by some 50 per cent in amounts as a percentage of the total federal budget.
Given this reality, and given the promise in the Speech from the Throne that the government plans, "a program of action would be designed to promote national development and policy that provides jobs, stimulates growth and builds regional strengths", how can the government do as it promised without the money being there to do that job?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT FINANCIAL SUPPORT FOR DREE PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the job can be done by increased expenditures if, at the same time, the government either increases revenues or, alternatively, cuts out existing programs or, additionally, increases the deficit. There is no magic way to the destination the hon. member has described for the House.
Oral Questions
It is from among these options that the government must choose in order to reach, not only the objectives of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion but other ministers of the government who are putting forward increased spending programs which cannot be met at the present time unless we increase projected expenditures much beyond the present projection, which was thoroughly criticized as being extravagant by members opposite.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT FINANCIAL SUPPORT FOR DREE PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Deputy Prime Minister cannot have it both ways: he cannot claim there is not enough money to do the job, and simultaneously build up false hopes in Atlantic Canada that the job is being done. That is what the government is trying to do.
Since the Premier of Nova Scotia and the president of the Sydney Steel Corporation have just recently expressed grave concern that unless the $50 million promised by this government-and the minister has already told us he is from the region-to Sysco is soon forthcoming, 400 more jobs are going to be lost, is the minister at least going to live up to his party's commitment made in the recent campaign to provide that money for people who want jobs, not hand-outs?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister of Finance and, if you will permit, I should like to follow it with a brief question to the Minister of Agriculture. In view of the widely recognized fact that the capital gains tax is daily destroying family farms and small businesses, particularly on their transfer from parents to children, and in view of the fact that the Crosbie budget of December 13, 1979, provided capital gains tax relief from that date and a parliamentary committee to review the whole question, why did the minister completely ignore in his budget of April 21 both relief from capital gains tax and measures to set up a parliamentary committee to review the whole question?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING RELIEF FROM CAPITAL GAINS TAX-READJUSTMENT OF VALUATION DAY
speechtext:

these proposals made by the former minister of finance were not being proceeded with at the present time, but that in the meantime we would produce a discussion paper which would go into the whole question of capital gains and the role it plays. It occurred to me it would be better to have discussion prior to new measures, instead of introducing new measures and then having the discussion.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING RELIEF FROM CAPITAL GAINS TAX-READJUSTMENT OF VALUATION DAY
speechtext: My supplementary is to the Minister of Agriculture. The farmers of western Canada look to him for leadership.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING RELIEF FROM CAPITAL GAINS TAX-READJUSTMENT OF VALUATION DAY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING RELIEF FROM CAPITAL GAINS TAX-READJUSTMENT OF VALUATION DAY

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF NEW CUSTOMS REGULATIONS ON SMALL BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Revenue. I might mention in passing that from what the Minister of Finance said today, it sounds like DREE again stands for "department for re-election expenses."
On the one hand, this so-called new Liberal government talks about helping small businessmen and, on the other hand, harasses them with new customs regulations like B-32 actions. Is the minister aware of what is going on in his department and the effect that this has on companies which can be forced to close their doors within 30 days because of the implications of that regulation?

speakeroldname: Hon. William Rompkey (Minister of National Revenue):
subsubtopic: EFFECT OF NEW CUSTOMS REGULATIONS ON SMALL BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for giving me notice of his question.
It is true that we have up to a two-year period to re-examine duty and tariff classifications. This is because we need the time to do research in the host country to make sure we are being fair. We do give the importer notice of this reclassification and, if he feels aggrieved, there is an appeal procedure.
It is not the intention of this government to harm small business but, rather, to encourage it, as my hon. colleague is doing. I will take the hon. member's question as a representation and make sure that we apply the law fairly.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF NEW CUSTOMS REGULATIONS ON SMALL BUSINESSES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, is the minister aware that it is possible to get three different classification judgments on one item by three different officers? If that happens within his department, how is it possible after two years to pass on those extra expenses from those extra tariff charges which now have to be affixed to the cost of the product? How can that be passed on by the company in order to recoup its expenses and still make a profit so that it can pay that tariff?

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF NEW CUSTOMS REGULATIONS ON SMALL BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I understand the difficulty which the hon. member presents but, as I say, we need that time to make sure that the duty and tariff classification is fair. There are a number of people who have the authority to reclassify, including the deputy minister and the dominion customs appraiser.
I just want to say to the hon. member again that I certainly will take his representation very seriously and make sure we are applying the law fairly and in the best interests of small business.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Bockstael (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: AIRLINE TICKET SALES
speechtext:
1. Generally, the answer is yes. In the case of international and transborder travel to the United States, the scheduled airlines have established, via their international and North American industry associations, standard rates of sales commission to travel agents. In practice, these commissions can sometimes vary according to sales volume, although this is not recognized by most of the airline industry as a legitimate procedure. For domestic travel, Canada's scheduled airlines have not established standard commission rates via their domestic industry association. Nonetheless, a uniform commission rate for such travel has resulted among the major airlines. The case of charter air travel is different, as commissions are paid by the charterer (tour operator) rather than by the airline. Commissions for charter travel differ from those for scheduled travel.
2. Section 112(10) of the Air Carrier Regulations (Consolidated Regulations of Canada 1978, c.3 states: "no air carrier, or any officer or agent thereof' shall offer air transportation at a toll or condition different from those set out in the air carrier's tariff on file with the Canadian Transport Commission (CTC), unless prior exemption has been received from the CTC. The CTC does not have direct jurisdiction over travel agents, however, and the legal applicability of this regulation to the actions of travel agents has not been fully ascertained. In the case of charter air travel, the airlines are not allowed to sell tickets directly to the public. Retail prices are set by the charterer or tour operator. Although travel agents normally abide by such prices, it is not certain whether they are legally required to do so.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS

speechtext: The House resumed, from Thursday, May 1, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bussieres (for the Minister of Finance) that Bill C-6, to revise the Bank Act, to amend the Quebec Savings Banks Act and the Bank of Canada Act, to establish the Canadian Payments Association and to amend other acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when I rose on this matter last Thursday, I had only two or three minutes before the time of adjournment, so at that time 1 made some reference to some of the comments made by the New Democratic Party. I hope they will look at those comments because I think they are important when we think about this piece of legislation, which has been before the House of Commons on so many occasions already, a piece of legislation which really forms, as the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) said, the charter and the basic working documents on which our banks operate.
The committee which thoroughly studied this bill when it was labelled C-15 in the Thirtieth Parliament was a committee that is no longer representative of this House in that at least ten members of that committee are no longer members of this House; and looking at the members who formed that committee, four of the members who remain as members of this House are now ministers of the Crown in the government in this Thirty-second Parliament. In all probability they will not be taking part in committee hearings. Nonetheless, before this bill goes to committee I think it is important that every member of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs thoroughly study the hearings and the representations made by various witnesses called by that committee, because it strikes me that the committee has done an excellent job in determining and making recommendations concerning this act.
Unfortunately there have been a number of economic changes in Canada since the spring of 1979. At that time we were appalled at prime rates being charged by the chartered banks of 12 per cent. We were appalled at that level of interest rates. Since that date and in less than a year interest rates have gone to 16.5 per cent, have been higher than that, and
Bank Act
perhaps have settled down to that, but are still in excess by 33 per cent above what they were at the time the committee heard witnesses from the banks and other Financial institutions.
There are a number of matters which perhaps should be studied by the committee before this bill is finally passed into law. In that sense I think we should study very carefully the past testimony and then hear from the officials of the ministry as to why certain of the recommendations made by that committee were not followed through when the bill was presented as it is presented now. Second, we should hear witnesses with respect to specific issues which seem now to have arisen that perhaps were not of concern or serious concern to the committee when it studied the bill in 1979.
I might suggest that those concerns are with respect to the activities of foreign banks. I think there has been a bit of a change in attitude. Certainly this government, in presenting its statement in the Speech from the Throne, indicated that it wished to take a much stronger pro-Canadian stand. Perhaps the government should explain very carefully to us in the finance committee why the strong pro-Canada stand indicated in the Speech from the Throne is not repeated in the suggested terms respecting foreign banks as set out in the bill.
A number of concerns have been expressed very dramatically recently with respect to automobile leasing and I would say with respect to other types of consumption-oriented leasing. The activities of the banks have been to some extent shown up over the past year. I want to deal rather in detail with respect to this leasing problem and to make the suggestion that it is imperative that the committee, in studying the act, thoroughly reconsider its position with respect to leasing.
Concerns have been expressed by Canadian cattlemen and there are certain other concerns regarding liquidity, and particularly with the problems which minor trust companies are having in this country today. It may well be that we should examine the extent to which banks should be entitled to stay in the mortgage field or in the long-term finance field, in view of the liquidity problem that massive changes in the interest rate structure such as have taken place over the last year in particular might create, impairing the safety and the ability of our banking system to continue to serve us well.
I might say at the outset that it is my view, and the view of members of this party, that the banking system in Canada is one of the finest banking systems in the world. It is important that that banking system be viable, that it grow, that it continue to serve Canadians and serve them well.
The committee dealing with this matter a year ago made reference to the need to define what is banking. The hon. member for Edmonton West made many remarks with regard to that matter and he was severely criticized by the hon. member for Burin-St. George's (Mr. Simmons) in debate. It was unfortunate that the hon. member for Burin-St. George's had not even had the Bank Act or any of the committee's reports. Indeed, he really did not know what they contained
710

May 5, 1980
Bank Act
and admitted to this House that he was speaking largely from ignorance. However, that is the hon. member for Burin-St. George's.
With respect to the definition of banking, it is, indeed, surprising to me, as it must be to all members of this House, that under Section 91 of the British North America Act the federal responsibility in respect of this whole issue is clearly defined in five separate paragraphs, including banking, the incorporation of banks, the issuance of paper money, interest, legal tender, bills of exchange, promissory notes and, indeed, even savings banks. These represent specific federal powers. It is a specific list of federal powers that certainly must encompass all of the concerns in respect of money, money management and financial management at every level.
However, the response to the insistence by the House that a definition of "banking" be included in the bill was this. The House had insisted that there be a definition of banking. The ministerial comment was that a narrow definition would overly restrict the activities of banks and their development, and a broad definition could result in some extension of banking legislation into areas of provincial jurisdiction. Having read what is clearly in section 91, I do not see how the provinces have any jurisdiction whatsoever in this field, save perhaps in a minor way under their property and civil rights powers.
What has happened is that this federal government has refused over the years since confederation to really develop its powers under section 91 of the BN A Act. It has let other jurisdiction into the field, more or less by the incorporation of provincial trust companies and a provincial mix, if you want, of mortgage and investment corporations, lending and land corporations, and a whole stream of other types of institutions which, by their very growth, have become what are commonly called "near banks". They take deposits, they issue current accounts, they cash cheques on demand, they treat themselves entirely as banks and they operate totally unregulated by this government.
To suggest that to define banking would unduly interfere with provincial legislation is to indicate that this government is prepared to abandon its true field, as set out by the fathers of confederation in the British North America Act. Yet, at the same time, the problems that we have in respect of national unity in this country really boil down to an intrusion into provincial powers by this government when we legislate on health and welfare matters, on cultural matters and on a whole host of matters which, on anybody's analysis, must be matters of provincial jurisdiction. We should be using the jurisdiction we have and that is properly identified with this government to legislate on matters of economics, to make sure the money supply is controlled, and to make sure we are doing the things we are supposed to be doing.
The other day the governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Bouey, issued a release to the major banks asking them not to make loans to enable U.S.-based companies to do an end run around U.S. credit controls.
One of the most important reasons the federal government is
in charge of financial matters of this nature, with powers set
out in section 91 of the BN A Act, is in order that the federal government can have fiscal control throughout the country. With the abrogation of federal responsibility, with the refusal to define "banking", and with the refusal-because we might get into someone's way-to act sensibly and in accordance with the constitution, we have allowed all sorts of situations in which the federal government can no longer fulfil its function. While the federal government can direct the banks, it cannot direct the trust companies, preventing them from making fancy transfers of foreign exchange from this country.
One of our problems in respect of interest rates is that there seems to be no way we can control foreign exchange matters. We wind up with problems concerning the balance of payments, and we have a situation in which we are told we cannot have our interest rates differ unduly from those of the United States. The reason, of course, is that we have refused to come to grips with the real constitutional requirement of having the banks and the entire financial structure totally under federal control. We have sat back and said we cannot interfere with matters of provincial jurisdiction. I think it is about time we started interfering with this matter and took ourselves out of some other matters where we should not have been in the first place.
The same question was asked in respect of what is a deposit. In this regard the minister's response was that it has not been possible to find a definition that is sufficiently flexible to account for present and future variations. Isn't that fine? We cannot even define a deposit! The reason is that the government says a deposit cannot be flexibly defined. It is obviously necessary, if we are going to control banking and determine what a bank can or cannot do, and if we are going to determine what those not licensed can or cannot do, that we define the word "banking", the business of banking and what is a deposit. We have to do that and we should do it now.
1 want now to deal for a moment with some of the problems concerning automobile dealers. I thought perhaps for the enlightenment of the House I would read four short lines of poetry as follows:
Through the open window's space Behold, a camel thrust his face.
"My nose is cold," he meekly cried,
"Oh, let me warm it by thy side."
That is just about what has happened in respect of our banking system and how it has managed to creep into almost every field of endeavour. We have been told in regard to leasing that it is important that the bank be available to use the leasing structure in order to finance massive capital purchases, and that this was the same as making regular, ordinary loans, just as they make commercial or household loans. For a moment let us consider the household lending field.
In the previous act banks were permitted to go into consumer lending activity. They went into it with full force. That was to make it easier for the ordinary person to borrow the money he needs in order to operate his home. Unfortunately, it became more than just that. There has recently been a flood of plastic cards across the country and there are big signs which
May 5, 1980

say "Yes" or "We candu". I do not know whether the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) had something to do with that "Candu", but the Royal Bank now has "Candu". The effect of all these monster advertising programs is that the banking system has tended to become a merchandising system. The Bank of Commerce now talks about a "boots and saddles" loan or they advertise "Can't we get you a new car?". The question is whether this is banking or merchandising-whether Visa, Master Charge and the others are just merchandising or a form of advertising of the goods and services produced by the business community.
We must consider the question of leasing, Mr. Speaker. It appears that the banks have decided to get into this field and a number of us are concerned about that. I can easily see how important it is that people who need to buy large capital items like dump trucks, front-end loaders, airplanes and such things, should also have the opportunity to lease them. This is the type of financial transaction that we expect from the banks. But then the question arises, are we going to be able to lease suits, chainsaws, automobiles, pleasure sailboats, surf boards-that sort of thing? Leasing could have the effect of encouraging some people to go further into debt. I am not at all happy that leasing the type of things I have mentioned is an activity that the banking community should be involved in. It is really merchandising.
The banks have stated in their presentation-and clause 193 of the bill sets this out-that they can only be involved in financial lease. This gives rise to the question of when a financial lease ends and when a maintenance or repair lease, for instance, ends. What distinction is made between an ordinary consumer item and a large capital item that might be used in business?
1 think it is essential, Mr. Speaker, that we examine the way financial leasing is being handled by a leading company, a subsidiary of the Royal Bank of Canada called RoyLease Limited. In the old act there was no provision for a bank to hold a company like RoyLease, although they were permitted to do so by a special order in council, more or less, pending revision of the Bank Act. Now all of the major banks have some sort of leasing arm and it is perhaps unfair to single out RoyLease. However, the hon. member for Broadview-Green-wood (Mr. Rae) has already mentioned this company and certain letters that have come into our hands which indicate that, while a bank is prohibited from going into maintenance leasing agreements-a situation where the renter of a car has maintenance included in his rental payments-that has not prevented RoyLease from insisting upon specific arrangements with specific garages.
This is what has been done with Mr. Lawrence Myers of Forbes Chevrolet-Oldsmobile Ltd. in Dartmouth, Nova Scotia. RoyLease insisted on an agreement for a 20 per cent discount on parts and a 10 per cent discount on labour. This was to be done through a special Visa card with a RoyLease sticker on it. The letter ends:
Bank Act
If this is acceptable to you, please sign and return this proposal to: Mr. Karl S. Aboud,
Automotive Services Manager,
RoyLease Fleet Leasing Service,
I Place Ville Marie.
This type of thing indicates that the banks in Canada are prepared to go beyond the normal and agreed "no maintenance" condition and "no licensing" condition and so on in a financial lease. It indicates that they are prepared to use tactics which may be described by some as strongarm tactics with respect to maintenance and purchasing.
The camel appears to have gone into the tent, Mr. Speaker. Automobile dealers express concern that while they are forced to borrow money from the banks in the normal commercial manner in order to finance inventory and receivables, the banks then force them to turn over their list of customers and list of receivables like any other business. The dealers are concerned that once the banks have the names of the customers and the amount of the lease of the vehicle, their customers will then become the banks' customers and that they, the dealers, will not be able to do anything about it because they still have to operate on a line of credit from the banks and co-operate with the banks or be left out in the cold.
We must address this question, Mr. Speaker. Surely there is a conflict of interest when the lender can also be the merchant. These are the most powerful lenders in the country. A current statement shows that at the end of February the Royal Bank of Canada had assets of $55.7 billion, the Bank of Commerce had assets of $49.3 billion and the smallest of the big five had nearly $30 billion in assets. And they should be big and powerful institutions, Mr. Speaker, capable of financing the commerce of Canada, but that should not be an excuse for getting into the merchandising of everything in the country.
It occurs to me that the camel in the tent has a cold nose, Mr. Speaker. Unfortunately he is a pretty big camel. Indeed, one camel is the size of $55 billion, so when he gets into the tent there is not going to be room for the automobile dealer! Maybe the end result will be that more and more consumer items will be financed by our lending institutions.
This brings me to our concern with residual values, Mr. Speaker. Certain draft regulations were produced by the former government regarding leasing, but unfortunately they are not contained in Bill C-6 as presented by the government. We were surprised that these provisions are not in the bill as they were in the previous one, Bill C-14. The committee had insisted that leasing regulations be posted and contained in the material presented to the House. We are sorry that the regulations are not there and we will be insisting that they be included, because they determine how leasing will operate.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the break for supper I was referring to the regulations propounded with respect to Bill C-14 before the previous Parliament, and those regulations stipulated that a lending institution, a bank, must provide in its leasing arrangements that the residual value of the leased equipment could be no greater than 20 per cent of the cost of acquisition of the property by the leasing corporation. Those regulations, and regulations like that, were referred to in a hearing before the Federal Reserve Bank in the United States with respect to bank holding companies in 1976.
In the United States there is an arrangement under the American consumer protection laws, and particularly under the consumer leasing act passed by the Congress of the United States on March 23, 1976, which specifically requires leasing corporations, if they are banks, to make sure that the residual value of the equipment being leased is the fair market value. In the event that at the maturity of the lease the equipment being leased is not the fair market value, the lessor of the equipment is not required to pay, if that is the case. So there is a real control to make certain that the leasing company makes sure that the residual value of the equipment being leased is in fact a fair residual value.
Clearly, the residual value is very important in determining the monthly rentals. If the residual value is estimated as being much higher than it reasonably could be in the normal case, then the rent charged can be considerably less than fair, and the American law makes that provision to protect the lessee of the equipment. One of the things we must concern ourselves with if we are going to allow the banks to get into the leasing field is to have regulations that ensure that the rental charged by the bank is a fair estimate. Our suggested regulations in October or November of last year with respect to the previous bill mentioned a residual amount not greater than 20 per cent of the acquisition cost.
I want to refer to what is in fact happening. I am taking some details out of a RoyLease lease with respect to a Chevrolet automobile where the original purchase price in the lease is quoted at $7,074.60. At the end of 24 months the vehicle is supposed to have a value of $3,256.74, or about 40 per cent of the value. That is the kind of lease that is being ordered by the Royal Bank of Canada through RoyLease in contravention of the regulations that were supposed to be in place with respect to this bill when this bill was before the House in the last Parliament. Indeed, it is not until the vehicle has been in the possession of the lessee for 36 months that the residual value of the vehicle is down to $1,345.16, which is just less than the 20 per cent requirement.
The point I am making is that the regulations as propounded in October or November of last year that have not been propounded by this government, and I make that point very clear, must be propounded by this government before this bill is to pass. However, those regulations have not been complied with by RoyLease, at least in determining how automobile leases should be worked out. They are talking about residual values considerably in excess of 20 per cent in their proposals to customers. What we have to look at is the kind of protection that Americans provide with respect to their consumer leasing act. That type of protection to lessees of equipment should be provided in our statute and in our regulations.
The next item I want to deal with is with respect to foreign banking. The details of foreign banking are set out in sections 302 and following. These banks are to be called schedule B banks. The minister was quite proud when he presented the whole matter to the House. He said that in no case will foreign banks be allowed to dominate more than 8 per cent of the total business of banking in Canada. Hon. members will recall I made some comments with regard to what is banking. The act does not define that. How the heck do you determine what is 8 per cent of the total?
When we brought the Mercantile Bank into Canada, it was not supposed to get even close to 1 per cent of the total amount of banking in Canada. That was the suggestion by Mr. Edgar Benson, minister of finance at the time. At the present time the Mercantile Bank has 1.5 per cent of the banking in Canada, so the growth factor is almost uncontrollable.
The practical matter is that once a bank is given a licence to operate in Canada, there is no practical way the Minister of Finance or indeed the Minister of State for Finance can in any way limit the percentage of business or percentage of gross assets that bank can have in Canada. Once you let the camel in the tent, it is totally impossible to tell how far the camel will go in the tent.
This government has made a great pretence of looking at a redefined Foreign Investment Review Agency, but we have a particular provision with the pious hope that you can limit foreign banking to 8 per cent. What has been the pious hope in the past? The pious hope with every business in the past is that Canada has been very poor at controlling foreign investment. We have an act that in fact authorizes and even encourages
May 5, 1980

foreign investment. It is in ministerial discretion. Although the minister is to ensure that no bank increases its percentage of business beyond 8 per cent, I doubt whether that is totally possible to enforce.
Once banks get in the position of taking business, they will continue to increase it. The minister can be as pious as he wants about 8 per cent, but once he starts making bilateral deals with other countries about banks coming in and doing business in Canada, what is he going to say to an applicant from Japan, for example? Will he say that we already have 9 per cent foreign investment in banking so you cannot come in, or is he going to say we will amend the act to make it 10, 15 or 20 per cent. The answer is that there is no way, unless we are going to have total government control over the expansion of competing banks, for the Minister of Finance or any minister or government to regulate a particular bank specifically to a particular size of the market place.
The whole concept is to bring foreign banks in to improve competition. This particular suggestion of 8 per cent is totally unworkable and the minister knows this. It is there because it may be interesting to talk about today when we have not yet got there, but eventually we will get 8 per cent, 10 per cent, 15 per cent or 20 per cent, and the statute will go on to 50 per cent, we know where it will go from there. The answer is that there is no way of controlling this percentage, and the minister should know that. He has no regulation that will allow him to discriminate from one country's bank to another country's bank and so on.
One of the other problems that involves foreign banking was brought to my attention by an officer of the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce with whom I had lunch, with respect to this.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
I thank hon. members of this House. Unfortunately, I was interrupted three times. I can promise hon. members I will not exceed in the true sense the full 40 minutes allotted to me. I appreciate the opportunity to continue.
As I was saying, the matter concerning foreign banks was brought to my attention by an official of the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce. He said that what in fact will happen is that the foreign banks will skim. They will come into Canada and take the good business, the easy-to-get business. He said that the foreign banks will not put an office in Inuvik, Frobisher Bay, or some small community that really needs banking services to cash old age pension cheques and so on. You will only find them in the big cities. They are going to take the easy-to-get business. They are going to skim. The foreign banks are not going to make the small business loans. I spoke
Bank Act
about that a week ago Monday. I am not sure that that act is worth anything.
The foreign banks will not make that kind of loan. They will not make the student loans. They will not do all the little things required of them. They are not going to pay any attention to the Minister of Finance when he wants certain things done in Canada. They are going to skim.
There is no provision in this act and the regulations concerning foreign banks to make them do the things that are socially acceptable in Canada. It is not possible to enforce such regulations. When they get in here, they take the easy-to-get business, the big business, the big buck deals that pay big bucks for them. They can repatriate their profits, but there is nothing in the act to make them do the socially acceptable things. In act after act passed by this parliament with respect to farmers, with respect to small business, with respect to students, requiring banks to advance the various easy or guaranteed loans for which we have provided, what will make the foreign bank advance those loans? That is skimming, and if we allow foreign banks in the country, surely we must provide in the charter that such banks take a fair share of the social responsibility which the large banks in this country have willingly accepted.
If we look at the Bank of Commerce, if we look at the Royal Bank, or the Bank of Nova Scotia, we find that they have willingly accepted social responsibilities. If new banks are to come into this country they must be particularly required to accept such responsibilities. It has been said that the schedule II banks will attempt to discourage the suitcase banker. It is said in the statute that we can stop his activities by not allowing him to conduct business. Unfortunately, the act does not define banking, so a company can come in here as the XYZ financial corporation, incorporated, say, in the province of Ontario, and since there is no definition of banking the company can do almost everything except call itself a bank.
There is nothing in this statute, despite the restriction on the offering of guarantees, which in any way inhibits the ability of a person to come into Canada and effectively carry on banking. The minister might argue that some of the sections-and I quote them to him-stop foreign banks. The truth is that there is more than one way to become involved in banking. There is one way well open to Canadians to become involved in banking, and that is to lend money to Canadian corporations and the interest can be repatriated to the lender in a foreign country without withholding tax. It is very simple to incorporate John Brown Financial Services Limited in the Province of Ontario, having the money that supports John Brown Financial Services lent to John Brown Financial Services on a floating charge debenture with a high interest rate, and immediately the foreign bank is in business; it hasn't got a foreign shareholder, the owner is a nominal Canadian. But, in fact, that foreign bank would be able, under the laws of this country, no matter what this act says, to do banking business in Canada, so this in no way inhibits that activity.

May 5, 1980
Bank Act
1 said at the outset of my speech that the government has power under section 91 of the British North America Act, repeated and repeated under five separate headings, to control every aspect of banking. We refuse to define banking and refuse to interfere in the activity of foreign lenders coming into Canada and tearing our financial system apart for their own benefit. We refuse to use our federal powers in this area, and this bill does nothing to control the foreign banker who decides, for whatever reason, not to be registered as a section B bank. This is a serious defect in the bill and I say it is essential that we re-examine the whole subject of the Bank Act with respect to foreign banks.
The last thing 1 want to talk about briefly is a problem 1 have foreseen in the last year. Some ten years ago we allowed banks to become involved in the mortgage business. The mortgage business, by and large, involves long-term lending, and long-term lending should be backed up by long-term borrowing. Unfortunately, the activity of the banks is such that the banks have not engaged significantly in long-term borrowing though they have, in the mortgage field, engaged in long-term lending. The consequence is that the banks are presently receiving a return of about 10.25 per cent on their mortgage portfolios and are paying in excess of 12 per cent on their savings accounts, while charging business at a prime rate of 16.5 per cent and usually one or 2 per cent over prime- 17.5 per cent or 18 per cent or so. The banks are thus suffering a negative return on their mortgage capital and, as a consequence, are forced to charge more than perhaps they should charge on business in short-term loans.
It is essential in this review that we look at the long-term lending practices of banks to make sure they are balanced by long-term borrowing. There is not quite the same balancing of long-term borrowing against long-term lending in the banks as there has been in the trust companies. What we did when we allowed banks into the mortgage lending field was purportedly to save the consumer interest on mortgage loans. There has been no proof of that. The banks have cut mortgage rates by maybe a quarter of a per cent. We have in effect hurt the liquidity of our banking system and, by that action, increased the rate the business community must pay for the business loans that banks are really there to make to give us the employment we need, to finance the inventories, the receivables and so on. So it is important, when we analyse this activity over the last year with the enormous increase in interest rates, that we look very seriously at how the banks have used their mortgage accounts, how they have used their consumer loans accounts, and how in all probability the business community has in fact had to pay rates of interest in excess of what they should normally have had to pay, in order to balance the losses the banks were taking on their mortgage portfolios.
My suggestion is that the banks should restrict their mortgage business. Perhaps we do not need the amount of mortgage money we did need at one time in order to finance construction. It might well be that insurance companies and trust companies could solve that problem. It might well be that
the banks should no longer be in the mortgage business. The fact of the matter is that the banking business deals in short term deposits, demand deposits, deposits on three days' notice or whatever, and that money is being lent on long term, and the banks are not in the business of lending long, any more than anybody else is when they have to borrow short. This whole matter may seriously impair the liquidity of our banking system and while at the present time our banks are limited in the amount of mortgages they can take, if we continue to allow the expansion of long-term lending by the banks based on short-term borrowing we are likely to impair the liquidity of our banking system.
Again I want to emphasize that the banks have done a good job in Canada. Our banks are worldwide institutions which lend credit to Canadians throughout the world, and when Canadians say they bank at the Bank of Commerce or the Royal Bank of Canada, or the Toronto-Dominion Bank of Canada, those banks are well known. We are not in the situation in which the Americans unfortunately find themselves, with banks in every state and every city of all names, sizes and descriptions. We have institutions of which we can be proud. It is the job of parliament to make sure that those institutions are guided and developed and that they work in the interest of all Canadians.
In my view the chartered banks exist to provide a safe depository for funds of individuals and concerns and, within the limits of prudent banking practice, to make loans available to facilitate production and trade in Canada. That is the job of the banks. It is not the job of being a merchant or of promoting the sales of individual products or services. It is a job of providing a depository for funds and making sure that those funds are available for business and trade.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I listened to the hon. member opposite I wondered whatever happened to that initiative to have installed at the front of the House a large bell that 20 members of Parliament could approach, and ring.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext: It should be over here.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
If it were down there, I would want there to be 35 members who could ring it.
It reminded me of one of the main reasons why I wanted to participate in this debate, and that was because in a past Parliament I had the honour of being chairman of the finance committee, and such a large degree of consensus developed over the long period of time that this matter was before Parliament in one way or the other that I was hoping to be able to see the bill move very quickly through this procedure and finally lead to the decennial revision of the Bank Act only eight years after the period in which the revision ought to have occurred. Instead of it being a decennial revision we are having something like 18 years between revisions. That is undesirable. It was one of the reasons why I was hoping that the bill would move rather quickly.
May 5, 1980

The trouble is that banking is a subject of enormous interest and importance to the Canadian people. There is hardly a Canadian who does not for most of his life deal with one of the chartered banks and, if I may say so, the banking system of Canada is not, in my opinion, entirely satisfactory. Every Canadian has his own criticisms of it. Some of them are unjustified, but some of them are very much justified. It is a highly concentrated industry. It is an industry which offers the consumer very little real choice between the various institutions which are the chartered banks, and so each member who comes to this House has his own life experience with banks, he has all of the experiences of his constituents, he has all of the advice of the various groups which have made submissions to us, and it is very easy to have a long and serious debate at any time on the subject of banking.
What I would like to suggest, however, is that the time for that type of debate really should be regarded as being over, in view of what has happened with this set of banking proposals before Parliament. I was hoping that a degree of restraint would be shown by all hon. members which would permit this piece of legislation to go very quickly to committee and, having gone through the committee, to become law very quickly.
I ought to add that restraint is more to be expected from members who have been around for the last seven or eight years than from many newly elected members-and I think particularly of members in the NDP caucus which has so much new blood-who have not had a chance to participate themselves in the consideration of this particular Bank Act revision, and the enormous temptation that they will feel to consider it a brand new bill requiring all kinds of new consideration and prolonged hearings. In my opinion that would be a disservice to this piece of legislation and a disservice to the process which has preceded it. It would be a mistake.
Parliament first began and the government first began considering this revision back in 1974 when a white paper was put forward. It received an enormous amount of public interest. Many briefs were submitted. Letters were written to members of Parliament. Eventually legislation was brought forward which took account, at least, of the great deal of criticism which was made of earlier drafts, and then it was referred to the committee which, as I mentioned, I had the honour to chair. At the same time-in fact, even earlier-it had gone to the Senate and received very full consideration there. I believe three reports were prepared by the Senate.
In the years I have been a member of Parliament I cannot remember a major piece of legislation of this kind which was the subject of so much co-operation and participation by members of Parliament. I can recall in camera meetings of the House of Commons finance committee at a time when we were expecting an election to be called from moment to moment, and yet members of Parliament, with all of the priority of an impending election call, were willing to take time to come to in camera meetings of the committee where their constituents would never find out about their contributions and their efforts, and all because of the shared belief that we had that what we were doing was important, that it was important to
Bank Act
deal with a decennial revision on a timely basis and to deal with the provisions and the briefs which were before us, and that Parliament and our country would be served by getting the job done, getting on with it and getting our report out.
It was not very long after our report was submitted that the government fell, and we looked forward in the next Parliament to seeing what the new Conservative government would do with the report of the parliamentary committee. Respect was paid by that government to the work which had been done by members of Parliament in the finance committee, and the legislation which was brought forward was right in line with our work and with our recommendations.
Now, of course, the Liberal government has returned, and we have just heard the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) criticizing the bill, as we heard last day when we heard the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) criticizing the bill. One wonders where they were in committee and in their own party when the legislation was brought forward at that time. The criticisms that they brought, as I said, are valid, are interesting and deserving of consideration, but surely we have reached the point where at least the Conservative party and the Liberal party should recognize a common commitment and a shared responsibility to see the legislation move forward, and not to re-open a great many old considerations.
I would like to deal in particular with the situation of foreign banks because I know there is much public concern about what is perceived as the entry of foreign banks into Canada. Those of us who were on the committee know perfectly well, as do most other Canadians, that in one way and another foreign banks are already here. When he spoke, the hon. member for Edmonton West was quite right in criticizing the absence of a definition of banking.
We undoubtedly have power in this Parliament to deal with the whole subject of banking, but the answer to that is that it is too late for the Parliament of Canada to assert that jurisdiction in the field and to define banking in a very broad and comprehensive way. The constitution does permit us to do it, but if we were to do it, our law would be paramount-that is, as I understand it, what happens in constitutional law-and we would overtake the operations and bring under federal control the operations of a number of institutions which are presently regulated by the provinces because, until now, the federal government has not asserted jurisdiction to cover the field completely.
The caisses populaires, the credit unions, many provincial trust companies which, in effect, carry on operations which could be defined as banking, and many other provincial institutions, would come under federal jurisdiction. I submit to the hon. member for Edmonton West and the others who hold the view that there should be a broad definition of banking in the act that, if we were to do that, we would create a minor, but important, constitutional confrontation with the provinces.
In the original legislation brought forward by the then minister of finance, the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien), monetary control was proposed to be asserted over

May 5, 1980
Bank Act
provincial institutions. That was found to be extremely objectionable to all the provincial governments, and eventually in the course of negotiation and on the advice of the governor of the Bank of Canada, the legislation was modified to withdraw from the confrontation and to assert less control over banking than I believe-and most constitutional experts believe-the federal government has. Now here we are-after having seen the bill revised, brought forward, approved, recommended on, and eventually a bill which deserves consensus having been brought forward-finding members going back to the fundamental argument that there should be a broad definition of banking. Surely it is too late for that kind of criticism.

speechtext: That is nonsense, and you know that.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext: If we had asserted a broad definition of banking many, many years ago, foreign banks would not be present in Canada in the way they are now.

speechtext: If you had exercised your jurisdiction, they would not be here either.

speechtext: That is an excuse.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
I have no doubt that if we had acted and defined banking back in the decennial revisions which took place back in those days, if they were here in Canada the foreign banks would be here on our terms, not on the terms which have been established by the various provincial governments. The credit union movement would be under federal control. But I regard that as a non-starter and I can hardly imagine that being put forward as a serious proposal by any members with any experience in federal-provincial relations, least of all members of the Conservative party who had the opportunity to provide a broad definition of banking when they were the government and who did not do it, for the very good reasons which I have just described.
The parliamentary committee recommended, and the Conservative and Liberal governments have responded positively, that the bill include a number of safeguards about the foreign banks. My friend opposite criticized the dangers of having the 8 per cent limit and wondered how it would be enforced. I think the 8 per cent limit will be easier to enforce than the controls which exist at present on foreign banks provincially. They are not really being controlled by this Parliament, and will be if this legislation moves quickly through Parliament. As I said, I hope it will.
There are other provisions which have been added to the legislation over the last two years of its consideration by this House to control the operations of foreign bank subsidiaries in
Canada. As I said, in my view these controls make the foreign banks more subject to federal regulation than they presently are, and it will make it easier to have a handle on their operations in this country than it presently is.
In order to allow the government to maintain a tighter control over the performance of foreign bank subsidiaries, the new bill provides for the licensing of such subsidiaries, which was the recommendation of our committee, with initial and renewal licences for periods of up to three years. The original bill did not propose any licensing or any review other than the decennial review of the Bank Act.
The new measure also redefines the proposed limit on the over-all size of foreign bank subsidiary operations in Canada. I think, frankly, the new proposals are more workable than the proposals that were put forward in the original legislation proposed by this government. It strengthens the prohibition against foreign banks operating in Canada except as subsidiaries, so as to encourage them to bring their Canadian operations under the supervision of the Bank Act.
It would remove the Bill C-15 ceiling limiting a foreign bank subsidiary to no more than five branches, but any branches in addition to the first would require ministerial approval to ensure the protection of Canadian-owned banks and to promote a wider regional distribution of such branches. This really is the answer to the criticism of the hon. member for Mississauga South that the foreign banks will come in and will skim the cream. I would assert that even in the areas where there is cream, more competition would be in order and would give a break to Canadian business and to Canadian consumers in giving them more choices of where to go. The formulation that is proposed in this legislation will permit the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) to say to a foreign bank which wants to come to Toronto, to Calgary, to Edmonton and to Montreal, "Have you looked at some other places where there is less competition than in these areas? Have you considered taking the responsibility of serving some of the regions in Canada which could benefit from it?" I do not think the response would always be negative.
I think that there are very good reasons why some foreign banks should go into some of the areas of this country where there is less economic activity because in those areas there is less competition. I think foreign banks will be able to offer quite a lot of new alternatives to the Canadian consumer and to Canadian business and they will cause important changes to take place within the Canadian banking system.
I know that during my years as a member of parliament we have seen the incorporation of some new Canadian-owned banks. When you look at the banking community and see how much concentration there is and how small is the number of banks in the field, you want more competition to take place. Of course Canadian competition would be better, if we could find a way of encouraging more Canadian banks to be established and to go into business.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
How do you help small Canadian banks?
May 5, 1980

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext: I am just coming to that point. The trouble is that in ten years of hoping and waiting, we have found that new Canadian banks are few and far between because it is very difficult to establish an institution that can compete with these giants which are already in the field. That is one of the justifications for giving the foreign banks more status here. If there were new Canadian banks, if there were an easy formula for creating another ten or fifteen substantial banks to offer competition with the banks to which the hon. member has referred, with the Toronto-Dominion Bank, with the Bank of Commerce, and so on, that would be another matter. But there is a lot of difficulty in establishing a new bank and competing with such enormous institutions. It is much easier for some large foreign banks to come in. They are in a better position to stand up to the heavy hitters that are presently in the Canadian economy. I am not worried about competition injuring the major banks which are here in Canada. I do not think foreign competition which will come in will damage them very substantially, if at all.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext: It will squish the little Canadian banks.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
What I see is that real competition will be provided and Canadian business and the consumer will get a better deal out of it. That is the main objective. We would like to see more domestic Canadian institutions grow and flourish. In fact the bill contains new provisions for facilitating entry into banking by new Canadian institutions. Let us hope that some major Canadian corporations that have a substantial financial base go into the banking business and offer to compete with the major banks. It has not happened in the past to any degree at all, but there have been some such cases. It will be easier for them do that under the legislation that is proposed. But I do not think that will provide enough competition or enough choice for Canadian business and for the Canadian consumer.
I should like to conclude now, Mr. Speaker. I will not ask for the indulgence of the House to continue unduly because I am trying to set an example of speaking briefly, recognizing everything that has been done by the last Parliament and the Parliament before that and the Parliament before that, as well as by all of the committees that have looked at the act and all of the briefs that have been submitted. Let us not think that now is the time to re-invent the wheel. We have legislation before us that many will criticize-there are many things you can say about it, many differences of opinion about it. The point is that if we go through a very long exercise, we will end up with something that will also be subject to criticism in many ways.
I think the interests of Parliament and the interests of the country are best served by regarding this legislation as something which is essentially in the nature of housekeeping, as something that members of Parliament should recognize as having already been worked on. Let us get this through and get on to some of our other business which is newly before this Parliament.
