subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak briefly on Bill C-6 and the Bank Act. As the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) pointed out last week, if we do not get this piece of legislation through, the banks will not be able to open their doors this coming July because it will not be legal for them to do so. The way the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) was going on, I thought he was going to blame R. B. Bennett for this delay in the Bank Act, but it is actually the cause of the previous Liberal government in the Thirtieth Parliament which procrastinated with the Bank Act. The Liberals in those days seemed to be having some problems with the caisses populaires in Quebec. I hope they have cleared up their problems so that we can get this piece of legislation out of the House and into committee.
Now I wish to speak briefly with regard to credit unions, caisses populaires, and some of their concerns with regard to the Bank Act. I see they have received some very well-deserved recognition this week in the April edition of Focus, in which an article stated the following:
Credit where it's Due
Caisses populaires and credit unions have worked hard to rise from grass roots to riches.
The emergence in recent years of credit unions and caisses populaires as major competitors with the banks and other financial institutions for consumer deposits and loans has given the movement a unique "banking" status.
In fact the Toronto-based Canadian Co-operative Credit Society Ltd., which provides financial and support services for 2,200 credit unions and caisses populaires outside Quebec, had examined the possibility of seeking a federal charter to form a full-service bank of its own.
The Bank Act, however, in its present form, Bill C-6, does not provide the mechanism to fit the credit unions into the federal regulated banking system. That was said by George S. May, the chief executive officer of the CCCS. The article continues:
Besides, the credit unions have developed "almost the same powers" as the banks, so the organization concluded there is really no reason to look further into forming a chartered bank.
Without reading the whole article, I should like to refer to the brief warning of Mr. May contained in the last paragraph, which reads as follows:
Commenting on the decade ahead. May says credit union expansion is not likely to be as marked as it was in recent years. Because of wildly fluctuating interest rates and our failure to conquer inflation, he says, "for any financial institution it is a time for consolidation, to take a conservative approach to growth."
We hope that the credit unions will have a hearing at the committee meetings. Many of us will be meeting with credit union members this week to hear their concerns. This should also help us in committee when we are considering Bill C-6. The credit unions have prepared an excellent document on some of their concerns and wishes. I should like to read a couple of them into the record. In the credit union document entitled "Banks and Banking Law Revision Act", they have stated the following:
The credit union system has supported the proposals encompassed in the government's banking legislation and urges their early adoption.

May 5, 1980
Bank Act
The credit union movement would benefit from the proposal in the bill to create a new Canadian Payments Association through which, for the first time, non-bank financial institutions that accept chequable deposits would be permitted to participate directly in the clearing system.
The credit union movement supports rapid passage of the new legislation for the following reasons:
(a)	It is in keeping with the government's stated intention to provide more equitable competition within the Canadian financial system;
(b)	Credit unions require equal access to the CPA in order to protect their future competitive position, especially since the CPA will become the focus for the evolution of electronic funds transfer systems;
(c)	Although the present clearing system, controlled exclusively by the chartered banks appears to work efficiently, there is no indication that it is cost effective from the point of view of credit union system;
(d)	Direct access by near-banks to the clearing system has been recommended by the Commons finance committee in its 1967 report on the Bank Act, by the Porter Royal Commission on Banking in 1964 and by the Economic Council of Canada in its 1976 study of deposit-taking institutions.
As the credit union movement has devoted considerable resources during the past four years to preparing for its proposed participation in the Canadian Payments Association, further delay would cause additional hardship and inconvenience.
They are experiencing enough problems right now with high interest rates which are the direct cause of the Liberal-NDP coalition in the Twenty-ninth Parliament when all limits on spending were lifted. Of course this caused the spiral and the eventual result today of high interest rate problems due to the high interest rate policy of the coalition in the Twenty-ninth Parliament.
The document continues:
In addition, other less controversial legislation, guiding the market behaviour of such financial institutions as trust and investment companies and credit union centrals, is being seriously delayed pending resolution of the banking legislation. It is time to get on with this work.
I will sit down now. 1 hope we will get on with this work in committee in the very near future.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me to take part in this debate as a new member of Parliament, although almost a veteran after 11 months, of course. Perhaps the question that concerns me as much as anything else, to begin with, arises from the previous Liberal speaker who suggested that there may be an attempt by new members of Parliament to hold up this particular piece of legislation. When the bill was first introduced they mentioned a great deal of concern about how this particular bill had been introduced three times in three different parliaments. They stressed a need to push the bill through, a great urgency to get rolling with it. I would suggest that many of the people who sit here feel that the real need is to take a very careful look at this particular legislation.
Our feeling is that there are some important changes here which will substantially alter the business of banking in Canada. In addition, we have had three elections, and certainly there have been some very significant changes in the composition of the House of Commons. There are new people here representing new ideas. Who knows? It may just have
been the Bank Act presented by Liberal and Conservative governments that was a determining factor.
There are new situations in the world which would justify a more careful look at this particular piece of legislation. We have seen interest rates take dramatic and unacceptable rises. We have seen oil prices driven up far beyond what they were when this particular legislation was introduced. We have seen the decline of the United States as a major and dominant economic force. We have seen the national debt go up astronomically. We have seen bank profits increasing in spite of economic recession. I would suggest that these are all relatively new things since that particular bill was introduced, and that what it really justifies is a new and more careful look.
A need for a new approach is important also. We have looked at the question of the philosophy of banking in this country as represented by the other two parties, as a very serious matter. But I think the members in these particular benches feel that this legislation should be dealt with effectively and efficiently. There is the question of some very objectionable sections in it that might, by informal discussion, be dealt with, rather than in the typical confrontation that has taken place in many parliaments here.
1 was very pleased to hear not many weeks ago when they discussed the banking legislation that the government would be open to amendments. I think this was a move forward. If in fact this legislation is to go forward quickly, I would suggest that perhaps there should be some discussion about the more objectionable features in it and an openness toward those amendments. I am sure as we move forward to committee that the matter will be considered seriously. If this kind of a procedure is followed, no doubt good legislation will develop which can be accepted by the majority of members in this House.
Maybe the reason we take such a vital concern in this piece of legislation, whether there is a fear on the benches opposite that this will be held up, is that from our point of view banking is a privilege, as indeed is any other corporation in this country. Through the corporate procedure risk is reduced in order to earn a profit, but banks seem to have the best of both worlds-a zero risk and excellent profits. 1 do not personally recall when the last bank failed, and I do not personally recall when the last bank failed to pay a dividend. But I am quite certain that all of us here are concerned about the social responsibility of those corporations, particularly whether we should allow foreign corporations into this country.
In our opinion, banking is one of the safest activities. We have made it that way in the Parliament of Canada, and for that privilege we expect a return to the people. We want some control on bank profits. We want banks to align their financial power with social goals that are held by Canadians. Banking, from our point of view, has tremendous power in shaping the Canadian economy. All corporations, all goods that are produced, and all services depend upon these particular banks. All employment and the shape of the economy in the future will be determined by these banks, and we are seriously concerned
May 5, 1980

that this legislation be given adequate consideration in this House and in the committee.
As a previous Liberal speaker mentioned, banks touch everyone and everyone has personal experience with them, but not all satisfactory. When the banking committee sits here in Ottawa members often hear from bankers and occasionally from other organizations, but they do not reach the people who live in Comox-Powell River, northern Canada, or in many other places throughout this country. We are concerned that when this legislation is considered it be given adequate consideration by all members of the House. We do not see the urgency in passing this legislation, but we do see the need for careful planning for the future and a thorough examination of this particular piece of legislation. Governments have changed and members have changed. Of course, 1 did mention the accessibility of the particular committee which studies this to all the people in the country.
I think perhaps one of the themes is that we could proceed quickly by co-operation. I mentioned previously the possibility of informal discussion about objectionable procedures and about agreements on some amendments. I also believe that this particular piece of legislation, since there will be extensive debate on it and work in the committee, will probably set the tone for the Thirty-second Parliament, and I would suggest that we all see a sense of importance in this legislation, with a willingness to co-operate and see it through. We should do that with the theme that we need a thorough examination, and in that regard I would suggest the government probably has two particular options, a plan (a) and a plan (b), if you will.
Plan (a) is what we have seen so often in the past; forced passage, forced sittings, Committee of the Whole rather than, as was suggested the other day, allowing the opportunity for members to question expert witnesses, and then, eventually, closure. It is kind of a war measures approach to passing legislation. Again, the urgency concern that has been expresed on the other side of the House worries me. We may find this to be a reaffirmation of the old arrogant, inflexible government approach.
The government's plan (b) could be another option, a new look. We would suggest that the present legislation be extended for a period of six months. We suggest that the government should lay all its cards pertaining to this piece of legislation on the table and allow an opportunity for serious consideration with a fair hearing. Through this process of co-operation we might find that we could do a better job in order to represent the people who are very concerned about this legislation.
This business of holding off and having the government lay all its cards on the table is of great concern to us. Bank profits have been a concern in the past. It is my understanding that the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is studying mechanisms that might control bank profits. Apparently that department is seriously concerned and is looking at the whole question of interest rate spreads. It is very important
Bank Act
that we have access to the material that is generated by those studies before we pass this particular legislative item.
The Post Office is studying the possibility of becoming involved in some banking services. It is my understanding that this has been done in other countries. We have had experience in this country with post office banking during wartime.
Im my particular riding, and this might be of interest to hon. members opposite, banks have withdrawn from communities. There are now communities in my riding and in other ridings where banking services are not provided to the people. The banks have closed branches and they are not accessible to the people. There are only about 7,000 bank branches in the country, but there are 8,000 post office outlets. It might be relevant for the Post Office to become involved in some banking functions, providing competition through the public sector. This would also provide involvement through the federal government.
By and large I think the main concern is that we want all the cards laid on the table. What is the federal government considering, and what plans does it have in this area? We should have that information before we put that stamp of approval on this piece of legislation.
Another area of concern involves foreign investment guidelines. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) has suggested we are going to seek guidelines for the performance of foreign corporations. I would like to see these guidelines clearly spelled out, indicating how they will apply to foreign banking institutions. If we are going to become involved with foreign banking operations within this country I think it is premature to pass this particular legislation before we know what kinds of goals for economic nationalism we are going to define, and what kinds of guidelines for the performance and operation of foreign corporations will be brought forward in this country. We should have all the cards on the table.
1 notice that the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) has dashed away, but even some of the things he might want to report to this House on, such as the activities of foreign banks involved with the Central Intelligence Agency, or activities in foreign countries, we might consider questionable.
There are certainly a great number of things the government is looking at now that should be laid before Parliament before we become involved in making a decision on this legislative item. There appears to be a great deal more information that members could have in order to deal with it effectively.
There are many areas in this act which we, in our party, feel could be improved. For example, I think of alternatives to incorporating banks by letters patent. That should be the subject of serious concern. We are concerned about the possibility of deleting the power of the banks to become involved in other areas of enterprise. We are seriously concerned about the control of corporate concentration in the banking industry, and we are particularly concerned about the prohibition on bank directors from sitting on the boards of directors of other corporations, or possibly holding other elected offices. We are

May 5, 1980
Bank Act
concerned about provisions for making more effective disclosure of financial information, and we are concerned about a policy and a procedure being developed to assist banks to help Canadians attain important national goals.
We listened to the previous speaker outline what a tremendous role banks have played in helping Canadians achieve those social goals, and how foreign corporations might fail to do this. I suggest to you there are many people in this country who feel that the social obligations of banks have not been met. I suggest that banks provide one of the classic illustrations of this failure. It has often been said by small businessmen, fishermen and farmers, that in order to obtain money from the banks you first have to prove that you do not need it. They really do not serve the kinds of needs we are looking at.
We would like to see programs to assist with regional development and assist in decentralization of economic decision making. We would like to give some powers to the provinces to become more involved in banking. We would like to provide mechanisms for consumer protection, and the involvement of consumers in the decision-making process.
As the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae) suggested, we would like to see a fair labour relations program followed by the banking industry, that last bastion of reaction in this country. We would, of course, like to see greater assistance for small businesses, farmers and fishermen.
We have a great deal of concern about the structure of the Canadian Payments Association. Finally, we have a very, very serious concern about and an objection to allowing foreign banks to function within Canada.
Perhaps just a comment or two about each one of these points might be appropriate. First let me refer to incorporation by letters patents. This, undoubtedly, is of great convenience and would allow foreign banks quicker access to Canada with the formation of new banks here. There is a serious need for competition in this field, considering the structure of the five major banks and the stranglehold they have on the Canadian economy. 1 would suggest that at the same time this procedure allows for a loss of accountability for the people of Canada. The function of banking, rather than being considered by the elected representatives of the people, then becomes less direct. It is streamed by the director general of banks through the Bank of Canada, through the minister of finance, through cabinet, and eventually to Parliament. With so many other things to take into account it seems there is a tendency to move away from the elected representatives of the people to consider the basic businesses that affect them. That is concentrated in the hands of cabinet and the prime minister's office.
Then there is the whole question of information to consider. There appear to be attempts to get safeguards to provide people with the information they need if we were to allow the incorporation by letters patent. I suggest this has been difficult in the past and to date we have not seen much action on the whole question of freedom of information. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it may even be a little premature to consider this
bill until the freedom of information legislation has come before us. People must be able to obtain the information they need in order to make judgments about the whole incorporation procedure.
When this legislation was introduced several days ago I recognized the phrase "trust us-we will round it out and flash it up in the regulations." I do not believe that history will bear out the fact that this is what happens. One would have been very naive indeed to trust some of the former governments of this country! As far as the entire procedure of incorporating by letters patent is concerned, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say to the government-non, merci. The charter by Parliament will safeguard the interests of the people.
Then there is the question of involvement in interests other than banking. This subject has been dealt with at great length, Mr. Speaker. There is some fear that leasing will put banks in a position to establish a beachhead in other businesses and then that beachhead will become the next area for expansion. We will see them in one area now, in another area later, and see them gradually expanding their business interests. Banks are probably the most efficient corporations that exist, but that is only because they happen to control access to money. If we allow them, they will eliminate competition; they will expand their business. Their profits-which are already enormous in the eyes of many people-would allow for cross-subsidization and the destruction of competition.
This tremendous market power should be checked; this capability to destroy a competitive system and loss of protection to consumers should be checked. We feel it is a conflict of interest to allow banks to consider loans to their competitors. Considering loans is the primary function of a bank-not going into other areas of enterprise.
Another matter to be concerned about is corporate concentration. It is interesting to note that the Bryce commission, which paid lip service to the task of examining corporate concentration in Canada, came to some of the most amazing conclusions. These corporate apologists, however, even singled out the banks for special consideration and critical comment.
In spite of the ease with which the government is allowing banks to form, or hopes that they will form, increased competition is virtually impossible because of the size of the market already controlled by the Big Five. From 1920 until the present, bank assets ran 80 to 90 per cent; in 1976 the Big Five controlled $108 billion of $121 billion in assets. It is difficult to see how any corporation no matter how easily it forms- except possibly the large multinationals-is going to enter the banking business and supply serious competition to the entire business.
In 1976 the Big Five had a majority of the branches throughout Canada. There were 7,018 branches altogether and the Big Five controlled more than 6,000 of them while all the other banks together had less than 1,000 branches.
It is very difficult to see how any corporation can be competitive in the banking industry in Canada. No matter what we do to provide competition, it is still akin to a closely
May 5, 1980

controlled economy. As I understand the theory of workable competition in a free market economy, it is that many small firms have easy access to the market place in order to compete, and that competition will not have any influence without limiting the size and scope of the activity of these major corporations. That is impossible.
There are some things to be said about the control of corporate concentration in this industry, Mr. Speaker. In 1976 a white paper dealt with the whole question of disclosure and the Bryce commission paid special attention to banks and the question of disclosure. It advocated greater disclosure in order to meet the needs of the people.
The United States is far less timid than we in this area. When we want information about a Canadian corporation, we no longer attempt to find out from the government or the corporate headquarters in Canada; we ask in the United States where they have adequate disclosure facilities and are not afraid to ask corporations to show what they are involved in. If Canadians want to find out the salary of the chairman of the CPR they can get the answer from the United States where they are not afraid of disclosure and where the provisions that apply to banks are much broader than in this country. I do not know what we or the banks have to fear, Mr. Speaker, so 1 urge that the provisions for disclosure in this legislation be dramatically expanded.
The Bank of America, for instance, has voluntary guidelines and some of the principles they are prepared to follow are worth noting. Customers for deposit services of the Bank of America are entitled to the information necessary to understand, evaluate the terms, conditions, availability and safety of the services provided. Borrowers are entitled to know the standards for credit eligibility and all information necessary to evaluate the credit extended, including all charges, and the methods by which they are calculated, as well as the conditions and obligations involved.
Investors in securities of the Bank of America corporation and its subsidiaries are entitled to the information necessary to judge the quality of their investments, the adequacy of the management and the value of their holdings. Employees of the Bank of America's companies are entitled to the information necessary to make informed decisions about their pursuit of personal objectives within the organization. Customers for the specialized financial services provided by the Bank of America are entitled to information needed to evaluate the terms, conditions, and quality of the services offered.
The vendors, suppliers and other businesses with which the bank deals are entitled to the information necessary to make sound business contracts with the corporation. This includes information about policies and agreements, transactions, competitive practices, non-discrimination practices and standards of fairness. The Bank of America believes that the public is entitled to the information necessary to judge the value and adequacy of the bank's contribution to economic and social well-being and its adherence to legal and ethical standards.
It is interesting to note that this government and its predecessors do not seem to recognize the necessity to provide
Bank Act
citizens of this country, the employers and users of banking services, with the kind of information that is supplied in the United States. That is very disappointing, Mr. Speaker; it is objectionable and should be changed.
While on the subject of corporate concentration and attempting to control it for fairness and equity in the marketplace, the whole question of bank directorships should be considered. For many years the problem of interlocking directorships has been a matter for serious concern. We find that there are bank directors on the boards of all major corporations in this country. We are disappointed that this legislation will not prevent that state of affairs. As we see it, it would probably be desirable to bar bank directors and bank managers from the boards of other corporations. This criticism has been met with the argument that such people provide tremendous insights when operating a business or providing financial services. I would suggest to the government that such advice can be obtained in a banker-client relationship. In that particular relationship, if you provide those services through a client-relationship, you do not run the risk of conflict of interest or coercion. Therefore it would probably be advisable if we provide greater privilege and power to bankers to eliminate the conflict of interest or coercion.
Moving from the subject of corporate concentration, which is of particular concern, to one of social responsibilities, there is a very serious question about social responsibilities of the banking community. We have heard a number of previous speakers attest to the great job they are doing, and certainly if the measurement strictly of profit is an indicator of great success in our society, then possibly the Big Five are tremendous successes; and we have guaranteed that for them. I have mentioned previously that in return for giving that guarantee and privilege, we would like to see the exercise of responsibility.
In some of the areas there are many national goals that we all look forward to achieving in this House, as do a great many Canadians. I would suggest maybe a few of them have been preached by many sides, the Conservatives and the Liberals, as they in turn form governments. We talked about a national goal and an industrial strategy in this country. We talked about an employment strategy. I have heard representatives from both parties stand up and say they had a goal of putting Canadians back to work. We agree with these goals. They are both vitally important goals, that is to say, getting that industrial strategy under way and getting employment created. As early as today we heard about the need of regional development to provide funds in this country, in northern Canada, in western Canada, in Atlantic Canada and in Quebec. This was to provide support for areas that through a period of time have not developed in a balanced manner. Regional development is an important national goal.
Then we come to transportation and communications. Apart from the tongue in cheek double-tracking escapade during the last election campaign, there is certainly a great need for

May 5, 1980
Bank Act
improvement in transportation, for example, the Prince Rupert port. There is needed a whole series of improvements and upgrading in the business of transportation and communications. These are national goals with which most people in this chamber would agree.
Now I would like to turn to increasing Canadian participation and control over our own economy. The last election saw the people who now sit in government in front of Canadians saying once again that Canadians must control and make decisions that affect the economy. There is too great a penetration of foreign decision making in this economy. Canadian nationalism and the economy were a great thing.
We can see parts of the country where housing is now in difficult straits. It seems to me that I read in the local paper about the "AFLOP" program and about zero vacancy rates in the area where 1 live. Housing is a very serious and important national goal which many of us share. The point is that we cannot keep fuelling these programs out of the public purse. The banks control an enormous amount of the nation's capital; they must become more involved and must bring their financial power to work together to achieve those national goals in a rational way.
In this House we have all said that we want to see an expanded and strengthened small business and middle-sized business program. I would suggest that no one is being hammered harder than those particular segments. Throughout the last election, and prior to it, a stream of small businessmen came through my constituency office. There was a tremendous volume of mail about the hardship which was being created by rising interest rates, especially in rural Canada where not only do small businessmen have to carry a large inventory, which does not turn over very quickly, but they must face high interest rates on that inventory. They have to face increasing transportation costs, strictly because of the oil pricing policy. The are faced with these two elements as well as a not too often sympathetic banking industry. In my riding I have had a number of experiences, and I am certain that everyone else has, where the bank has arrived on the doorstep of the small businessman and said, "My auditor just came in today. I have too many loans out. Your loan with our bank is chopped." And that was it.
One business successful for many years, with 80 employees, had the vice- president of the bank from Vancouver along with the local branch manager arrive in the office with no notice and say to the business people, "We are calling the half a million dollar loan that you have out." The gentleman replied, "I run a very important business that serves the coast of British Columbia, not just the 80 people employed in this community and all the services and maintenance we require from this area." The bank representative said "Tough." He was asked why. The bank representative said, "We have no explanation, and we are not required to give one. It is a demand loan. Goodbye. Pay the money." And that was it. That is not a very socially responsible approach. These small businessmen are faced with high interest rates, stifling freight rates, and a banking industry which can come to their doors
and say that its auditors said there are too many loans out, and that they are picked to go down the drain.

We would all like to see a more socially responsible approach, that those who consume the services of the banks in this country would have more protection, access for appeal and reconsideration, not just a blank "thank you very much, that is a demand loan and we want all the money back today regardless of the consequence on your firm, its employees and services it provides to the people of rural Canada."
We are talking about national goals and, if I may be permitted to stretch it a bit, we all want a Canadian merchant fleet. We have talked at length about that in this House. It almost came to pass. We want to see the shipbuilding industry improved. Again, it should not all be borne out of the public purse. The banks have an obligation to bring their financial muscle behind that program and we should be encouraging that through stated policies in this legislation.
In my particular riding, and in the area of B.C. that I represent along with many other members who sit in this House in two particular parties at this moment, we are concerned about the Indian communities. Time and time again leaders of the Indian communities have come in desperate need for access to capital. They are told by the government to go out and make plans. Those communities that plan properly will be given access to capital to carry out those plans. 1 submit that Indian communities have done a tremendous amount of planning and hoping. They want the kinds of benefits that are available in other communities. Every time they arrive on the doorstep for assistance from the government for access to capital, they are told to go and whistle.
The banks could play a substantial role, with the assistance of public direction, in providing the desperately needed capital in Indian communities. It would be interesting to see the government comment on a situation like that. These communities need housing. They need developments in their infrastructure. Basically they need capital for economic development to put Indian people back to work. It is an interesting side feature that we do not really seriously consider Indian employment in terms of things they are able to develop and promote and improve themselves. We do not even include Indian unemployment in our statistics, and yet it is a most serious unemployment situation in my riding and in the ridings of many people from that area.
There has not been much social responsibility in banking, not because the banks are basically evil or malicious, but the lust for profit is there. If the banks are allowed the opportunity, they will certainly follow the path of least resistance to reach that profit. Development in the areas I have talked about is vital to a balanced development of the Canadian economy. Unfortunately, they are not the most profitable and they even carry a slightly greater risk. Through this particular
May 5, 1980

piece of legislation I think that we could encourage the banks to participate more fully in developing and balancing the economy of Canada.
A further question is the one of consumer protection. We mentioned the whole business of disclosure of information. Perhaps I might be permitted a moment to take a look at the entire question of consumer protection in relation to banking.
Consumers who are users of the banking system can make intelligent choices about the services only when working with adequate information. Under consumer protection we feel that banks must disclose for the individual consumer in that bank, general credit policies and lending guidelines, all terms and conditions for borrowers including related and additional charges, for depositors the terms and conditions of savings accounts or other savings instruments such as RRSPs, all terms and conditions of mortgage lending, general advertising policies, policies of providing information to creditors, credit agencies or others, policy of retaining customer records and maintaining confidentiality.
Another question about consumer protection is the entire business of the credit card industry. It appears today that the banks, through the promotion of convenience credit, have more than 10 million cards in the hands of Canadians. About 48 per cent of the respondents to a Canadian Consumers' Association survey in Toronto in 1975 said they had experienced billing problems with their cards. Only 61 per cent of those errors were corrected within a month. The number of personal bankruptcies in 1978 was 15,800. Did you say good?

The question of the credit card system will fuel the whole business of inflation. It will increase bankruptcies. This type of credit should be provided as is necessary. You can holler all you like. Look at the record. It is there. For some new member to come into the House and say that since 1976 this matter has not had an adequate airing in the House of Commons and has not been heard adequately, is a lot of nonsense. It has been heard. I hope that the House will act with a certain amount of dispatch after it gets rid of a couple of items that seem to be bothering us, and let the Bank Act get on its way and into operation. I believe the passage of the Bank Act is more important than the minister's budget, whenever he brings the other half of it down. This is the engine. This is what makes our business operate.
I want to deal with a couple of specific items in the Bank Act. My colleagues covered much of the hearings and the witnesses we had before us, as well as the submissions we received from foreign banks and so forth. I want to deal specifically with one section that we have changed. That is the old section 88 of the existing act which is now section 177 in the bill before us.
When we did some research on this portion of the act. We discovered how it had found its way into the Canadian act. It was lifted out of a British statute that went back to 1815 and had been substantially unchanged since that time. It was a means of allowing a manufacturer or producer to offer as collateral to the bank his work in progress or his raw materials.
A businessman may go into the bank and say to the bank manager that he wants to use section 88. As far as he is concerned, that is a form that the bank has which you fill out and sign. There is a lot of legalese and words in there, which he does not understand and I do not understand. He knows it has to be signed if you are going to pledge the work in progress or raw material as part of your collateral for the loan he is going to give you.
I think the minister is a reasonable person. What we were trying to bring before the committee was that commerce has changed a lot in this country since 1858 and that a large segment of our economy is now engaged in what I call loosely the buy-sell business-they buy material from various parts of
the country and from outside the country and they service and sell it to businessmen. They are faced with a particular problem today because the banks really have no way of taking their inventories as collateral except when they take a floating charge debenture. They allow them actually about 30 per cent of real value. A businessman, say, has $750,000 tied up in inventory upon which he will only get around $215,000 from the bank when it gives him an allowance for collateral purposes.
We find that in most other jurisdictions merchandisers, wholesale or retail, can go to the bank and upon convincing the manager of the quality and freshness of the inventory, can sometimes get 75 per cent or 80 per cent. That is a matter between the banker and a businessman. We have no mechanism for doing this. We suggested, and, fortunately, the members of the committee agreed, that we should amend section 88, and we have now added wholesale and retail services to that section as far as inventory is concerned.
I think few people realize how important it is that the wholesaler or the retailer now has available to him, provided he can get the auditor to verify the value of his inventory and the bank manager has adequate confidence in the businessman and his auditor, a medium of collateral beyond the 30 per cent he would normally get. If we can get this going it will do a tremendous amount for wholesale and retail trade in this country and will help a lot to prevent many of the bankruptcies which are now occurring since, in most cases, bankruptcies come about through lack of working capital.
Another thing a lot of people do not realize is that the cost of carrying inventory in past years used to be borne to some extent by the manufacturer. Today it is not carried by the manufacturer at all because of a change in the style of manufacturing. Hon. members may recall when President Nixon brought in the 10 per cent surcharge on imports and then, along with it, passed Disc legislation which allowed American companies which manufacture and sell to a Disc corporation to retain 50 per cent of the profits they made from exports interest-free, at the pleasure of the President. The effect has been to put into the pocket of the American manufacturers, in this case, a source of funding at no interest; members can imagine what assistance this is to a manufacturing company.
The American supplier utilizes this advantage by taking an order from a Canadian consumer or a Canadian wholesaler and trades it at the bank, using it as part of his justification for getting funds from his bank in the United States. He will take an order to his bank manager, supply a history of his client- how long he has been doing business with him and the history of his payment record-and is then able to get an advance of funds for the operation of his business. Then, when he produces his product, he does not put it in inventory; as soon as it comes out from the production line it is shipped, in this case to the Canadian wholesaler, and it is the wholesaler who carries the cost of the inventory. But you see, Mr. Speaker, the wholesaler has no way to react to these circumstances. He has no source of funds unless he wants to invest his own money in
May 5, 1980

the transaction. He has no way of getting funds through his bank to enable him to carry that inventory. So we were looking again at section 88, and that is another reason why we decided to amend it.
We heard a little rumble a year or so ago about section 177-we heard there were some people in the other place who were not very happy with it. In fact they wanted to change it back to the old section 88. They did not want that wording changed at all. As it turned out, the Canadian Retailers Association heard about the good things in section 177 and the Canadian Federation of Independent Businessmen heard about it too. They descended on Ottawa and wanted to meet with the banking committee in the other place to tell them a few of the facts of life about wholesaling and retailing in Canada. Of course members of the committee backed off when they saw there was some objection. We hope they have seen the light and that when the bill comes before their assembly they will allow it to pass without changing that section or sending it back to us for further debate.
I want to say something about leasing because we have had a number of discussions with the Canadian Federation of Automobile Dealers about leasing and about their concerns, particularly at the present time in the light of difficulties experienced by automobile dealers in coping with the downturn in the economy. A lot of the dealers tell us that about 25 per cent of their income is derived from leasing and they are very concerned that the banks intend to move into this field and take a good deal of it away from them. Indeed, when our hearings were going on, one of the chartered banks told us they were planning to place a leasing officer in every branch across the country and that they were actively going out to seek the leasing business.
As other members have mentioned, the Royal Bank of Canada has sought to line up dealers to supply them with automobiles at a few dollars over cost and perform service for them at a 20 per cent discount, or something along those lines. This is really not the business of the banks at all. So we intend to press the minister to get the leasing provisions amended. This is one of the few points we are concerned about-getting that leasing matter dealt with. We think leasing should stay with the dealers. We believe that automobiles and light trucks up to maybe 16,000 GPW should stay with the dealers, and that the heavy trucks and the large ticket items should be made available to the banks.
I might say that the Canadian Federation of Independent Businessmen has carried out a survey in the last month, I believe. The results were in today, and I understand that 67 per cent of the small businessmen across this country indicated in the ballot that they do not want to see the chartered banks in the leasing field. I think the minister is a reasonable person, and I believe he will listen to that opinion and accept an amendment which would allow the banks to stay out of the leasing field and not get as involved in it as they thought they were. Car dealers have told us that the banks in fact have been raiding some of the leasing companies and taking some of their
Bank Act
personnel, and that they are really ready to go into leasing in a big way. We think this is not a good move.
There was some concern expressed about the computer services that they were going to offer as well. I just bought a computer at my own business about a year ago. I recall going to the bank and telling them that we were buying. We had to talk to them because we were buying the computer, and it was quite expensive. They immediately said, "Well, why buy a computer; use our service". One of the things we have to remember is that we have to be flexible enough to move. We do not have to stay with one bank all the time. My concern was that if I had all my records tied up in the computer system of the bank and I wanted to move to another bank, I would have quite some difficulty doing that, so I chose to stay out of that and to use my own computer. Then, if I choose to go from one bank to another, I will.
I find that Canadian businessmen have a fixation about banks. Many of them come into my office, and they are always blaming everything on the banker. Sometimes it is the banker's fault, but it is not always his fault. Many times it is the businessman's fault. What I tell them is that if they have an idea and they are going to the bank for financing and they have it all written down and laid out so the banker can take it and explain to the people he has to deal with-maybe his regional manager or whoever it is above him who approves loans-he has to have something to pass on to him then. If the matter is explained in a reasonable way and the banker turns the applicant down, he should not become despondent. There are five or six other banks. He should just go to another one. If they all turn him down, he should go back and have a look at the concept of what he is doing. However, because someone turns him down, that is not the end of the line. I have been turned down many times, and sometimes when I have sat back and looked at it, I was glad I was turned down.
The fact is that if you do not try and do not venture, you should not blame the bank. If it turns you down, look at another one, refine your presentation and have another go at it.

subtopic: INDUSTRY-AID TO CHRYSLER CANADA-IMPACT ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT OF CANADA
INDUSTRY-AID TO CHRYSLER CANADA-IMPACT ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday, May 2, I asked the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) why he had apparently completely ignored the request of a successful, growing, Canadian-owned
May 5, 1980

company for aid in expanding its product line. His answer to this question was completely unsatisfactory. He ignored the question, and this, together with similar evasive answers by the minister over the past two or three weeks, has caused me to rise tonight to comment on this issue.
Let me put the matter in some perspective. First, the aid to Chrysler, rumoured to be in the range of $200 million to $250 million, compares with the programs of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Department of Regional Economic Expansion in the following way. The total budgetary and non-budgetary estimates for the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce were $508 million, and for DREE, $562 million. Of that amount in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, $200 million will be by way of grants and contributions. I ask the minister whether he had stopped to consider the impact of this Chrysler aid within his over-all budget. The Chrysler aid represents an enormous part of the budget in two key economic development departments.
Second, Chrysler has had a somewhat checkered existence in recent years. This is the third time that Chrysler has suffered financial problems in the past ten years. Each time the problem gets worse.
Clearly any aid to Chrysler Canada is very significant in relation to over-all Government of Canada industrial development programs. There is also significant risk that Chrysler will be back to the trough again. Thus the decision that the government makes must be viewed with concern since the decision made today may well be the precursor of a similar decision in the future.
1 have tried to obtain from the minister answers to the following questions. Out of what fiscal envelope will Chrysler aid be provided, the economic development envelope or the social welfare envelope? Will any aid to Chrysler have an adverse impact on other economic development programs? Putting it quite simply, will the provision of aid to Chrysler result in fewer economic development dollars being available for other programs? I have pointed out one unfortunate situation, that of CAE Industries, which was ignored completely by the minister. What is the significance of this lack of attention? Is the government considering any alternative ways of dealing with the very serious problem of lay-offs and long-term unemployment in the automobile industry?
The minister today made the ridiculous statement that he would report to the House by the time of the question period. To date he has said nothing to the House by the time of the question period. I have learned more about Chrysler from reading the newspapers. It is essential that we have a full debate in the House on the aid program. What impact will it have on small business? What impact will it have on high technology industry support? What impact will it have on other assistance in Ontario? What impact will it have on other parts of the country? These are all very important questions.
I can understand the reluctance of the minister in commenting on particular aspects of current negotiations, but I cannot understand him stonewalling me on these broader questions. Is there any reason for his attitude? Either the answers to these
Adjournment Debate
questions will arouse unfavourable comment from Canadians at large, or the minister has not directed his attention to them.
Prior to the election, and even since 1971, the Liberals have been calling for an industrial strategy in this country. What is that strategy and where does aid to Chrysler fit in it? It is sad to say that we are facing here one of the most significant economic development decisions that any government has made in this country, and there is no comprehensive economic strategy within which to judge the merits of the decision. I can only discuss the matter in the context of certain statements made by the minister and others on his side in recent days. Industrial strategy usually requires that aid be given to growing companies, to the winners. Chrysler is clearly not a winner. How, therefore, is aid to Chrysler being tailored to ensure that Chrysler will become a winner?
The hon. minister has championed the cause of Canadian-owned companies in his comments on industrial strategy. How does aid to Chrysler fit within these policies? Why has he ignored a growing, successful Canadian-owned company which needed a nominal amount of capital to provide 200 to 400 jobs and some $20 million to $30 million in new business? The inconsistency is alarming. It took a statement by the president of that company that the business had been lost to evoke any reaction from the minister.
Support for small business is, and always will be, a key to any sound industrial strategy. Will the aid to Chrysler inhibit the government from supporting small business? If the money available for small business is not forthcoming because of the aid provided to Chrysler, one can be sure that the outcome will be received in a very negative way by the small business community, and rightly so.
I have asked many questions. 1 have not in any way tried to disrupt the negotiations which are currently under way. The purpose of these questions is to try to understand the framework within which the government is making this very far-reaching decision. It is critically important that this be done prior to the decision being made. It is impossible now for Canadians to indicate whether or not they support in principle the aid to Chrysler, since they do not know what this aid entails.

subtopic: CULTURAL AFFAIRS-FUNDING OF VANCOUVER ART GALLERY
CULTURAL AFFAIRS-FUNDING OF VANCOUVER ART GALLERY
speechtext:
During the last few days I have been trying to determine, in question period, the intent of this government concerning certain commitments made by the previous administration on the financing of arts and sports projects from Loto Canada funds. I find the answers to these questions uninformative and unsatisfactory.
On April 22, I asked the Secretary of State and Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox) whether it was his intention to honour the commitment made by his predecessor to provide $4 million toward the conversion of the old court house into Vancouver's art gallery. In reply the minister indicated that such financial pledges were merely campaign commitments and that they were being reviewed as such.
On May 1, I asked the minister responsible for sports or the Secretary of State whether the government intended to cash the $6.4 million cheque that had been sent to the federal government by the provinces as the federal share of Loto Canada funds. In reply the minister responsible for sports indicated that the government did not intend to cash the cheque until the legal position of the agreement between the former administration and the provinces on Loto Canada had been established.
In reply to a supplementary question the Secretary of State
reaffirmed that any decision on the art gallery or similar
projects must await the possible jurisdictional dispute between
the federal government and the provinces over Loto-Canada. We might wait forever. The issue is very simple. Will the government meet the commitments of the former administration and put up the funds for these projects?
I am particularly concerned about the federal financing of the Vancouver art gallery. This cannot be dismissed as a campaign promise. The first request for federal funds for the art gallery was made two years ago to the former Liberal administration. Subsequently, nearly $12 million has been pledged from private donations and municipal and provincial pledges, all awaiting confirmation that the federal government will come through with the promised $4 million. If the federal government money is not forthwith coming we are in the ridiculous position of having to return to the private sector the $5 million that it has contributed for the art gallery.
For the record, I would like to read the chronology of the Vancouver art gallery funding. The timing of events is as follows. In 1978 the gallery requested $4.5 million from the Liberal government. The rationale for this request was that the federal government had made similar grants across the country, particularly for Montreal and for the Ontario art gallery in Toronto. Vancouver was the last major city to be without an adequate facility and it was not unreasonable to request funds from the federal government. The amount of the request was in the order of magnitude of those for other galleries, and it is our turn.
At the same time, in 1978, a request to the provincial government was made for a grant, plus the value of the land on which the old court house stands. Subsequently, Vancouver city committed funds from the sale of the present gallery site.
In 1979 the gallery went public to raise $2.5 million. The very successful "Take the art gallery to court" campaign was launched and actually raised $5 million from the enthusiastic citizens of Vancouver between April and August of 1979, of which $2.5 million was set aside for the purchase of Canadian art.
In January, 1980, the former secretary of state, David MacDonald, announced a grant totalling $4 million in the form of $1 million per year. At the end of March, 1980, the provincial government committed $2 million, contingent on federal government funds.
We now have a situation where nearly $12 million has been pledged for both the gallery and the art bank, all awaiting confirmation of the federal government's $4 million. The delay is costly. A conservative estimate is that the delay is costing us about $100,000 per month.
If the art gallery does not go ahead, Vancouver will lose employment opportunities in cultural industries, a show case for major exhibits, such as the King Tut exhibit which attracts tourists, $2.5 million in grants for the art bank, $2.5 million in private pledges, $2 million from the provincial government, the site of the old court house, and $4.6 million from the city of Vancouver.
May 5, 1980

Surely, Mr. Speaker, the time has come to end this uncertainty and proceed with this project now while these pledges are available.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Stollery (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State and Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications; Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CULTURAL AFFAIRS-FUNDING OF VANCOUVER ART GALLERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have this opportunity to clear up-1 would not go so far as to say misunderstandings-the thinking of the hon. member who just spoke. Her thoughts on this subject are not very clear. I should like to emphasize that we are dealing not with government commitments but with election promises. That is very much part of the problem.
During the election campaign the former secretary of state went across the country promising a great many things. I note there was $3 million for an art centre in Thunder Bay; $500,000 in Vancouver for the Waterfront Theatre, and another $4 million in Vancouver for the art gallery. That was all very nice, but these were election promises and nothing more. At no time did the Conservative cabinet commit themselves to these projects, and at no time did the previous government give the projects Treasury Board or cabinet approval. In fact if the hon. member would take the time to look again at the wording of the former minister's press release she will note that all that was said was that the former minister was "-prepared to allocate up to $4 million" under "-a proposed federal program." There was no commitment on the part of the former government-again, only election promises.
Even more important, Mr. Speaker, is a subject that has been brought up by the hon. member-the question of the fairness of the Loto Canada agreement. Under that agreement $12 million would be allocated to arts and culture. Was this, in fact, the best deal for the cultural community? Had this agreement with the provinces not been made, it is estimated that 30 per cent of the total net revenues from Loto Canada would have been allocated to arts and culture on an annual basis. Loto Canada estimated this amount at $30 million. Even a more conservative estimate, forecasting increased competition in the lottery field, would estimate the yield to arts and culture being no less than $19.5 million per year. In fact the arts and culture community lost financing during the period of the last government.
These figures must be taken into account, Mr. Speaker. The government must be sure that the Loto Canada agreement negotiated by the previous government was the best deal for the people of Canada and gives a fair share to both federal and provincial governments. As soon as the issue concerning the distribution of the Loto Canada funds is resolved, the government will be in a position to reassess the capital project requests that have come from across the country. I must point out to the House that there are over 60 applications outstanding for these funds. The government would be in a far better position to meet those requests if the previous government had
Adjournment Debate
not, through its Loto Canada agreement, reduced the funds that would have been available to the arts community from Loto Canada.

subtopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-REPORTED MERCURY POISONING OF NORTHERN ONTARIO AND QUEBEC RESIDENTS-ACTION TO PREVENT
HEALTH AND WELFARE-REPORTED MERCURY POISONING OF NORTHERN ONTARIO AND QUEBEC RESIDENTS-ACTION TO PREVENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the observations of a report published by the Department of Health and Welfare entitled "Methylmercury in Canada" about a month ago, states that mercury levels being found in some individuals in northern Ontario and northwestern Quebec are a significant health risk, and that it is probable that some may show early or mild symptoms of mercury poisoning. The report concluded that even though milder forms of mercury poisoning quite possibly are occurring, it is difficult to prove it conclusively.
On April 29, 1980, the McGill University study on the effects of methylmercury poisoning on the health of residents in certain Quebec Indian communities was released. It found that there was an association between some of the neurological findings and estimated exposure to methylmercury. More surveillance of the population was recommended, and I concur, Mr. Speaker. But, in the end, it is not enough to describe a problem well. The politics of description is the classic liberal, social, scientific approach to the problem. Description changes nothing; only action does that.
In reply to my question in the House the other day the minister said she would have to wait until this last report was released. It has been released now, and we on this side of the House expect an answer. Therefore, I ask again what new steps are the minister and her department taking to stop the systematic poisoning of residents in northern Ontario and northwestern Quebec.
Pollution of our environment, especially that pollution already there in damaging proportions, is one of the most difficult, most frustrating and most tragic problems that industrialized countries will likely ever have to face. Make no mistake about it, we will have to face it. To be fair to the government, there are no easy solutions. There is no invisible hand which will correct, what has been for a long time, a serious predicament for the residents of northern Ontario and northwestern Quebec.
The situation as I see it is this: that innumerable studies have shown inconclusive but nevertheless significant evidence that poisoning of the river systems of northern Ontario and northwestern Quebec by methylmercury has affected deleteriously the health of the native population of the area. We have two sets of facts before us that should move the government to meaningful action.
Lirst, we know that enormous amounts of mercury have been dumped and are continuing to be dumped into river systems. Second, we know that mercury poisoning causes certain types of symptoms, many of which have been observed

May 5, 1980
Adjournment Debate
in places like Grassy Narrows, White Dog, and Mistassini. We know from the Japanese experience the fact that Minimata disease frequently appears only after years and years of eating contaminated fish.
1 find myself wondering whether or not this government is going to act only when we do have conclusive scientific findings, when mental and physical abnormalities in children and adults can be proven to be caused by methylmercury poisoning. This burden of proof set-up that finds us in this, as in other environmental issues, waiting to die in order to prove that we are being killed, is morally depraved. It seems that society is willing to accept these risks, as they are euphemistically called, associated with its economic development and standard of living, and this government reflects this willingness to accept these risks. But risks to whom? In this case it is the powerless people who are on the periphery of our industrial society, almost untouched by its benefits but burdened with its wastes. While we unjustly force these people to take the present risks, 1 think it important to remind ourselves that if this madness keeps up we will all be forced to accept these kinds of risks in one way or another.
I wonder what would happen if our response to the problem would be any different if this situation were occurring in any one of our large cities? My guess is that the response would not be all that different. So charges of racism in this question are appropriate on the one hand but overplayed on the other, because no matter who the people are or how well they are integrated into our economy, their health would also be risked for the sake of a system that puts profits ahead of people. For all its ugliness, racism has at least a human quality. But what sort of inhuman system do we live in when nobody matters, when nothing interferes with the system? This indeed brings new meaning to the phrase "systematic poisoning".
I am not hopeful that this government will take meaningful action until it changes its attitude toward the problem of pollution and how to stop it. The government must stop describing the situation and start prescribing for it with courage and foresight. Instead, Liberal and Conservative federal and provincial governments have taken the view that the public should pay for the costs of suppressing industrial pollution because the public benefits from the reduction of pollution.
Liberal and Conservative governments use tax credits and public subsidies as instruments of policy to protect the environment. I submit that this is destroying our environment. It is no surprise that this government is continuing this dangerous path. For instance, witness the latest government giveaway to Great Lakes Forest Products Limited which recently bought out Reed Paper-of $38 million, $25.3 million from the Conservative government of Ontario and $12.7 million from this Liberal government in Ottawa, ostensibly to be used as an incentive grant to help rebuild its facilities at Dryden and Thunder Bay. I wonder if it is merely a coincidence that of the $335 million total program, $35 million will be spent on pollution abatement measures that-and I quote from a DREE press release:
-are expected to result in full compliance with the Ministry of Environment's requirements.
Is not the free market system wonderful? Is it not terrible how the government intervenes in the market place, and then only to bring full compliance after all these many years? We in the NDP believe that the polluter should pay the costs of suppressing pollution to protect the health of people and of the environment.
We must ask ourselves if we want the kind of society that places most of the risks of pollution on people who themselves do not pollute? Is it fair that it is us in the main stream of society who are the ones who generate disproportionately more pollution and the rich even more disproportionately, while governments act not to make the private sector pay the social costs on its activities, but instead pick up all the costs on behalf of the Canadian taxpayer?
Governments must act to redistribute not only the wealth of society more fairly, but also the risks to health and the costs of ill health. To do this, tough and enforced public regulation will be necessary along with compensation to the victims and efforts to rebuild broken lives through the development of alternate employment strategies. Governments that fail to do this by only monitoring the problem are as negligent and as guilty of destroying human health and the quality of life as the polluters themselves.

speakeroldname: Mr. David Weatherhead (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-REPORTED MERCURY POISONING OF NORTHERN ONTARIO AND QUEBEC RESIDENTS-ACTION TO PREVENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the findings of the departmental mercury program across Canada are described in the document "Methylmercury in Canada" which was released in March, 1980, and are supported by the findings of the McGill University study in northern Quebec, which was released on April 29, 1980. Both documents come to the conclusion that while severe methylmercury poisoning or Minimata disease has not been found in Canada, milder forms of mercury poisoning, although difficult to prove conclusively, quite possibly are occurring in certain areas.
There is no specific medical treatment for the effects of methylmercury, and health programs must, therefore, concentrate on identifying those who may be at risk, and on a preventative approach in the form of health education to help individuals avoid taking in a significant amount of mercury. Therefore, the following actions are under way.
First, at risk areas are being identified based on knowledge of mercury levels in native people and fish and sea mammals.
Second, surveillance programs will be continued in these at risk areas so as to assist individuals to modify their diet to keep their mercury levels within acceptable limits.
Third, health education programs will be continued in the at risk areas.
Fourth, it is important that careful balance be established between the advantage of the traditional Indian and Inuit way of life, which can provide an excellent source of dietary protein in the form of fish and sea mammals, and the potential danger
May 5, 1980

to health due to elevated mercury levels in that food source. Medical Services Branch staff are committed to work with communities and individuals to devise local solutions tailored to specific circumstances, needs and lifestyles.
Fifth, for successful local solutions, adequate information on mercury levels in local fish and sea mammal food sources must be available. Medical Services Branch staff will continue to facilitate obtaining this information from federal and provincial departments of fisheries.
Sixth, blood mercury levels estimations will become a standard investigation in the antenatal care of women from communities in at risk areas.
Seventh, the area of Quebec in which the McGill study was carried out is part of the area covered by the James Bay
Adjournment Debate
agreement, and ongoing care in that area will be undertaken by the Cree board of health. The board has already taken action to establish a task force to design the future program. The task force will have at its disposal both the departmental and the McGill mercury reports, and has been offered whatever assistance they may need from this department and le ministere des affaires sociales du Quebec.
1 am sure, Mr. Speaker, that this answers the question of the hon. member.

speechtext:
Mr. Prime Minister of Japan, Mr. Speaker of the Senate, Madam Speaker of the House of Commons, members of the Parliament of Canada.
On behalf of the people of Canada and of their parliamentary representatives, I have the honour to extend to you, Mr. Prime Minister, to Mrs. Ohira, to Foreign Minister Okita and to all the members of your entourage, a most cordial welcome.
This is indeed an historic moment. 1 note with pleasure and pride that you are the first holder of the high office of Prime Minister of Japan to address the Parliament of Canada.
